title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two separate pieces.

**(1) §53, the end of the preceding paper (p.156).** Let p = 2q+1 be prime. The numbers a counted here are those whose powers run through all residues. In modern terms they are the primitive roots mod p.
- Euler states that their number equals the number of integers below p that are coprime to 2q = p−1, i.e. φ(p−1).
- He recalls that he showed elsewhere how to compute this count by factoring. If 2q = f^ζ g^η h^θ k^κ, the count is (f−1)f^{ζ−1}(g−1)g^{η−1}(h−1)h^{θ−1}(k−1)k^{κ−1}. This is Euler's totient product formula.
- Given one primitive root a, and with 1, α, β, γ, … the exponents coprime to 2q, all primitive roots are a, a^α − np, a^β − np, …. That is, the least residues of a^α mod p for gcd(α, p−1) = 1.
- This is correct: the order of a^α is (p−1)/gcd(α, p−1), which equals p−1 exactly when gcd = 1.
- The existence of a primitive root is presupposed, not proved here.

**(2) Opening of E555 (p.157).** The problem of interpolation is stated: find a relation y(x) taking prescribed values p, q, r, s, … at x = a, b, c, d, …. Geometrically, find a curve through given points.
- Euler remarks, citing an earlier occasion, that even infinitely many points do not determine the curve. Infinitely many curves pass through the same points; in modern terms one can add any function vanishing at all the nodes, e.g. a multiple of sin πx for integer nodes.
- Hence any interpolation method gives a very particular solution. Its character depends on the chosen ansatz, i.e. the general form of the equation.
- This motivates the next page. There Euler restricts to odd series y = αx + βx³ + γx⁵ + …. He then uses a Newton-type divided-difference scheme in the variable x², with the basis x, x(x²−a²), x(x²−a²)(x²−b²), ….
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. §53 tacitly assumes a primitive root exists; this was not proved by Euler, and the first proofs came from Legendre and Gauss.

ideas.what: Number of primitive roots mod p equals φ(p−1); all primitive roots are a^α mod p with gcd(α, p−1) = 1
ideas.modern_name: Count of primitive roots / generators of the cyclic group (Z/pZ)*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler stated it (with the term 'radices primitivae'); Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801), gave rigorous existence
ideas.where_published: E449 (Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia, 1774) and E554, of which this is the ending

ideas.what: Product formula for the number of integers below N coprime to N
Interpolation through infinitely many points does not determine the function; the result depends on the chosen ansatz
ideas.modern_name: Non-uniqueness of interpolation of entire functions (cf. adding sin πx; Carlson's theorem as the later uniqueness criterion)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Commonplace in 18th-century interpolation discussions; uniqueness conditions due to Carlson (1914)
ideas.where_published: Euler's own back-reference ('alia occasione observavi'); also in his earlier work on interpolating series, e.g. E189 (unsure of exact locus)

ideas.what: Interpolation restricted to odd functions, ansatz y = αx + βx³ + …
ideas.modern_name: Odd polynomial interpolation / Newton divided differences in x²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Newton (divided differences); the odd specialization is standard

deep.surprise_reason: Both pieces are well documented. Euler's count of primitive roots via φ(p−1) and the totient formula are standard Euler credits. The non-uniqueness remark on interpolation is a known Euler observation that introduces E555.
transcription_corrections: 'curnam per ea transeuntem' should read 'curuam per ea transeuntem'.
'Haec formalis consideratio' is doubtful in the scan; it is likely 'Haec formulae' or a similar word, unsure.
In the §53 list, the first term is 'a' and the others are 'a^α − np; a^β − np; a^γ − np; a^δ − np; etc.', which matches the image.
